newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU officials eye breakthrough in Danish vote impasse.
newsitem.headline: EU officials eye breakthrough in Danish vote impasse.

text.p: European Union officials on Monday modified a proposal to counter Washington's anti-Cuba laws to make it acceptable to Denmark, but was waiting to see whether the 14 other members would agree the changes.
Diplomats said that after hours of consultation between legal experts, Denmark had agreed to a revised proposal to combat the Helms-Burton Act.
"We've practically broken their thumbs to get them to agree," said one diplomat. "It looks as if it has been tweaked and tuned in such a way as to be passed."
Denmark said it would veto the original proposal because it believes the part of the EU treaty they come under compromises national sovereignty.
Without giving details, however, diplomats said officials believed they had found a way around the impasse.
"It remains to be seen whether the rest will agree the changes," one diplomat said. They were due to vote on the issue later on Monday.
At issue was a response to the Helms-Burton Act -- an amalgamation of years of U.S. anti-Cuba policy.

Officials were concentrating on seeing if the reprisal measures could be passed using another section of the EU's treaty which might provide Denmark with a way out, although one diplomat said any final response would have to include the so-called Article 235 to which Copenhagen objects.
Danish Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said Copenhagen's "legal problems" remained over the article -- a catch-all clause which allows the EU to take action on behalf of its 15 members.
The Danish government is currently embroiled in a court case brought by a citizens' group that accuses it of handing too much sovereignty to the EU.
But diplomats say while this would have the same effect in protecting European interests, they fear the political message they wanted to send to Washington would be diluted.

Some diplomats had been hoping to persuade Denmark at least to abstain from voting on the matter, but other diplomats said this would be "like having a nuclear deterrent made out of cardboard missiles".
Brittan said if the EU failed to come up with a response, it would send "a very bad signal" to those who wish to interfere in Europe's affairs".
The proposals would allow countersuits to be brought anywhere in Europe against litigants who sue European companies or individuals for contravening the Helms-Burton Act.

Among other things the act allows naturalised Americans to take action in U.S. courts against "traffickers" -- foreign companies or individuals accused of gaining from investments made in property confiscated in Cuba since the 1959 Communist revolution.
The Danish decision will not affect a case brought by the Commission against the United States at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in Geneva.
A WTO panel is due to convene on November 20 to rule on EU complaints that the act -- and similar laws which seek to quash trade with Iran and Libya -- is extra-territorial.
The European Union is still studying proposals to bar U.S executives involved in litigation from the 15-nation bloc and has already begun compiling a "watchlist" of potential litigants.
